name: Seisan
description: An advanced kata with thirteen techniques and complex combinations of hard and soft movements.

origin.title: Origin
origin.content: Seisan is perhaps the oldest kata in Okinawa-te, and is found in both Shuri, Naha, and Tomari traditions. There are versions attributed to master Sokon Matsumura (Shuri) and to Higaonna (Naha), and even kanbun Uechi (Tomari). It probably dates from the late 18th or early 19th century, long before Miyagi, and originally comes from southeastern China (Tora-kenpo has a longer Seisan under the same name). After their China periods, Matsumura and Higaonna continued to teach it in Okinawa. In the Naha line, Seisho Aragaki taught Seisan to Higaonna before his journey, which indicates that the kata was deeply rooted in Okinawa. In Goju-Ryu, reference is often made to the Naha heritage that Higaonna learned this from Aragaki (who in turn learned from Matsumura). In short, Seisan is an ancient kata that has crossed both Okinawa and China.

transmission.title: Transmission to Goju-Ryu
transmission.content: Kanryō Higaonna adopted Seisan in the Naha-te and taught it to Miyagi. Miyagi spread it further in the Goju tradition. Others also brought Seisan (e.g., Takahara Peichin to Sakugawa). Thus the kata came into all Goju lines (also in Kyokushin, Isshin-Ryū, etc.). It is one of the core kata that Goju inherited from the original Naha-te.

historicalDevelopment.title: Historical Development
historicalDevelopment.content: Seisan remained relatively stable, albeit in various performances. There is no unambiguous "the true" Seisan, because each line (Matsumura/Shuri, Aragaki/Higaonna/Naha, Isshin, Uechi) developed its own versions. In Goju (Miyagi's line), the kata is hard/soft mixed with both striking and throwing and gripping techniques. After Matsumura's or Higaonna's journey, Miyagi introduced no major new changes; he learned the existing form. However, there was later an adaptation in Japan: Funakoshi changed Seisan to Shotokan as Hangetsu, but in Okinawa, Goju dojos have retained the original name. Over the years, the hard-soft combinations and triple repetitions remained characteristic.

technicalFeatures.title: Technical and Philosophical Characteristics
technicalFeatures.content: Seisan contains many double/triple strike combinations (techniques that occur three times in a row). The kata has a great variety of stiff and flowing techniques: gates of strikes, high elbows, strikes, throws, lock grips and even strangulations occur in it. It is not just strike-block work; there are also "escape" movements (escaping from grips) and nervous edge techniques. Philosophically, Seisan shows the complete arsenal of Goju-Ryu: it is both a strength and endurance kata. It is notorious for brutal applications: e.g., claw grips and "lobster claw-like" grips (similar to fish-hooking) to hit vital points. Due to the highly concentrated movements (Sanchin-dachi and cat stance), the kata requires much control.

controversy.title: Controversy/Variations within Goju-Ryu
controversy.content: There is much variation. Countless Okinawan masters can claim their version. The discussion focuses mainly on the name (13 vs "13 techniques"). Some point to a legendary master Seisan as a possible namesake. Funakoshi's change to Hangetsu in Japan is also remarkable. In the Goju circuit, there is no dispute about "the right Seisan": everyone practices their familiar version.

relationships.title: Relationship to Other Kata/Systems
relationships.content: Seisan is central to many Okinawan styles. In Shuri (Matsumura) it is called "Hangetsu" in Funakoshi's work. In Goju it is the 9th (or 10th) kata, usually for black belt. In Isshin-Ryū (Kyoda/Shima), Seisan is also present. In Kyokushin (Oyama) and Isshin it also has a place as a heavier kata. It shares much with Chinese Taiji and Shaolin Tiger/Crane combinations (the theory about Yuan Fei seishan in Shorin has some roots). Internally, Seisan is sometimes called "the mother of all kata" because of the complete teaching it contains.

modernPractice.title: Use in Modern Practice
modernPractice.content: Seisan is widely taught in Goju-ryu. It appears in kata competitions (Goju and open shori events) and is popular for stage demonstrations. In contemporary Goju, Seisan is seen as an ultimate test of technique and mental strength. It serves to train all aspects (strength, breathing, technique) and remains part of the highest curriculum in JKF Goju Kai and IOGKF.

nameAndMeaning.title: Name and Meaning
nameAndMeaning.content: Seisan simply means "thirteen". The Japanese kanji are (10) and (3). This is usually interpreted as "13 (killed?) techniques" or "13 combat movements". An alternative explanation is "10 and 3" where most techniques in the kata are repeated three times. Since the kanji (seishan) already existed before karate in Japan, it is uncertain whether the Okinawan original had a different meaning. The fact is that 13 is considered a lucky number in China, which some find relevant symbolism.
